text: The Exchange.
Harvest. Edrin, twelve years before the hard winter.
Whose autumn is it?
Abel Furrowe. Inspector for the exchange. He weighs what the town sells.

From the bell tower, at noon. The carts come in off the plain in a line that goes back past the mile stone, each one loaded higher than the one in front, and the drivers asleep on top with their hats over their faces because the horses know the way.
Every roof on Exchange Street has a chimney going, for the baking. You can smell the bread from up here.

Behind the mill, in the barn yards, the hill people who come down for the harvest. Washing on the ricks. A fire in a ring of stones with a black pot on it. Children in the stubble after the gleanings, and a dog going mad with happiness chasing nothing.

On top of the big rick at Haldane's, a man with his shirt off is singing while he forks, loud, in Heshen, and the men on the cart below him are laughing at him and shouting the chorus wrong on purpose.
A good year. Every cart is a good year.

The barns at Haldane's, before it's light. The hands sleep eleven to a barn on straw, and the first one up kicks the fire in the stone ring back to life and puts the black pot on it, and the smell of the oats gets everybody else up.

Ketti Sallis is up first, because she's always up first. She's got her hair tied up in a cloth and her sleeves pushed past the elbow, and her forearms are scratched to the wrist from the stubble, a hundred little lines, some old and some from yesterday.
Arn. Arn. It's the sun.
It's not the sun. That's the moon.
It's the sun and you owe me a penny.
I owe you nothing. I tied ninety-one.
Ninety-four. Old Tesk counted. Ask him.
Old Tesk, on his back in the straw with his hands folded on his chest like a dead bishop, says ninety-four without opening his eyes, and coughs, and turns over.
Arn finds a penny in his shirt and throws it at her and she catches it one-handed without looking, and puts it in her mouth for safekeeping, and goes on stirring the pot.

Davin, eight, is sitting on an upturned bucket by the fire with a crust, and Kel Tesk, fourteen, is sitting on the ground beside him teaching him to whistle through a split stalk of barley. Kel can get a note out of it like a curlew. Davin can get a noise out of it like a door.
You're blowing. Don't blow. Breathe at it.
I am breathing at it.
You're blowing at it like it's soup.

Davin tries again and coughs instead, and coughs, and Kel bangs him on the back, not gently, and then takes the stalk off him and does the curlew again, and Davin laughs with his mouth full and sprays crust on the fire.

Up on the end rick, Ilo is already working, with his shirt off in the cold, forking down for the first cart. He's singing. The hands below him come in on the chorus wrong on purpose, and he stops, and looks down at them, and starts it again from the top, slower, like a teacher.
He'll sing till his teeth drop out, that one.
He'll sing till Furrowe pays him.
Then he'll sing for ever.

Ketti doles out the oats into the tins, a big spoon each and a little spoon more for Kel, because he's growing, and he looks at the little spoon more and doesn't say anything, and eats it with his fingers before it's cool enough.

The exchange hall. Iron pillars painted green and a glass roof the pigeons get in through. The big scale in the middle of the floor, the beam level, a sack on one side and the brass weights on the other, and a man in an apron squinting at the pointer like it owes him money.

The price board on the end wall, chalked up fresh every hour. Barley, wheat, oats, by the sack. Under the oats, smaller, in a different chalk that has been rubbed out and written again a lot of times: HANDS, BY THE SACK TIED.
At the side gate the hands queue to be paid. Hill men, Hesh, with blue thread round their wrists and the chaff still in their hair. A clerk at a table counts coins into each palm and doesn't look up.
A boy with a broom is sweeping under the scale. Thin as a rake. He keeps his head down and sweeps the spilled grain into a little pile, very carefully, so none of it goes to waste.
Kel. Out the road of the gentlemen.
I'm doing under it, Mr Haig.
Do under it when they've gone.
Up in the gallery a man in shirtsleeves leans over the rail with a pencil and shouts the barley down to the telegraph boy, who runs.

Abel Furrowe does the round every day at eleven, with his good hat on, the new brass band on it so bright you can see the windows in it. He taps the scale. He reads the board. Men touch their caps and he touches his back.
Mr Furrowe. You'll want to see the back store, I suppose.
I'll want to see the back store, George, yes. I always want to see the back store.
Every day for nine years.
And every day it's grand.
Every day it's grand. Come on, then.
They like you. You can tell when a man likes you by how he complains about you.
Go round to the back store with him.
Orme's back store, behind the mill. Sacks to the roof, a lamp hung on a hook, the dust standing in the light like it's been put there. A leather strap on a nail by the door, black with hands.

Haig has Kel Tesk by the collar against the sacks. One of the boy's boots is off, on its side on the floor, and what's come out of it is barley. Sweepings. A double handful, and some of it is floor dust.
In his boots, Mr Orme. Both of them. Walking it out the gate a boot at a time.
It's off the floor. It's off the floor, I swept it. It was going on the midden.
Was it.
My dad's got it bad in his chest. It's only for a pudding.
George looks at the barley on the floor for a long time and doesn't say anything. Then he looks at Abel.
Floor sweepings go to the pigs at a farthing a bucket. That's what it's worth, if anybody's asking.

source.words: Go round to the back store with him.

text: Write it up, then. It's the rule now, or it will be on Thursday. I can't be seen.
Mr Orme. It's sweepings. Mr Orme.
I know what it is, son.
Kel is walked down to the post with a boot in each hand and his feet bare, and the barley is put in a paper bag and the bag is written on, EVIDENCE, and the date.

The boy is sent up the hill road that night with the paper pinned to his coat, barred off the plain. His father comes down the track to meet him, coughing, and they stand in the road a while and then go up together. At the mill, Haig sweeps the floor himself and puts the sweepings on the midden.

That night, on the hill track above the post. No moon. Kel coming up it in the dark with his bare feet, because the boots are in a paper at the post with the barley, written on. The track is flints and sheep muck and the first frost's not come yet, but the stones are cold enough.
By the turn at the gate his feet are cut on the soles in a dozen places, and every step he puts down leaves a dark mark on the stone that you'd see in the morning if anyone came looking.
Old Tesk is waiting at the gate with a lantern. He's come down from the fold with his chest, which took him an hour, and he's sitting on the wall with the lantern between his feet.
Where's your boots.
At the post. In a bag. They wrote on it.
What did they write.
I don't know. I can't read it, can I.
Old Tesk gets down off the wall and takes his own boots off, one, then the other, and puts them on the stone in front of the boy, and stands there on the flints in his stockings.
I'm not having your boots.
They're too small for me. They've always been too small for me. Put them on.
They go up together, the boy in the boots and the father in his stockings, with the lantern, and the light goes up the hill a turn at a time and goes over the top.
The registrar's upstairs room, on the Thursday. A long table with green baize gone bald at the elbows, a fire too big for the day, a decanter nobody has touched yet because the professor hasn't.

Round the table: the registrar, asleep with his eyes open. Edwin Mott with the minute book. George Orme. Dr Lind, who came in late and kept his gloves on. Clement Ashby from the Gazette by the window, for the press. Abel Furrowe for the exchange, with his hat on his knee. Josh Brack standing at the back by the door, because nobody asked him to sit.
And the guest, Professor Calley from Arlen, who has written a book about the hill people and has the book with him.

The wording, then, as drafted. That for the purposes of the poor rate and the relief, a resident of the district is a person with a fixed abode in the district at the first frost. And that a person engaged for the season is not resident by reason of the engagement.
Which means the hands.
Which means anyone engaged for the season, Mr Orme.
Which means the hands.
It has to be worded generally.
Am I wanted for this or not? I've a woman in the barns at Haldane's who's been coughing since the barley.
The board would like to know whether the hands carry fever down off the hill. For the minute.
They carry what everybody carries. They sleep eleven to a barn on wet straw because that's what the barns are. Put them in a house and they'll cough like a house.
I'll put that they present no special risk.
You'll put what I said.
Edwin writes something. It is shorter than what Lind said.
Mr Furrowe, for the exchange.
They wait for you. They always wait for you.
Say it: A tenant. A man renting a place. He'd be resident under that?
A tenant has a fixed abode. Yes.
Even a hill man.
The wording's general, Mr Furrowe.
So it is. Put the exchange down as content, then.
There's the barns at Haldane's standing empty since Purkiss went to his daughter's. You own them.
Professor Calley. The board would be glad of your view.
Oh, I'm only a guest. I'm here for the supper.
He waits to be asked again. The registrar wakes up and asks him again.

Well. I'd only say this. They don't want to be resident. That's the thing nobody here seems to grasp. You give a Hesh man a house and he'll be gone by Easter. They have the hill in them. I've stood in their villages. You've never seen people so cheerful with so little. I don't believe they think about next year at all.
They think about next year when I pay them.
Ha. Yes. Well, you would know.

Everyone laughs, Calley loudest. Ashby writes in his notebook. At the end of the table Edwin Mott writes the minute, and reads it back, and the registrar says carried, and nobody puts a hand up against it, and that's the whole of it. The decanter goes round.

The night the rule is passed. Josh Brack comes to the barns at ten with Will and a lantern and the post dog, Pilot, a brindle thing with half an ear, to count every hand who's sleeping on the plain and write them in the book for Mott's list. Every name in the book is a name on the list at the frost.

Ilo isn't in the book. He's been sleeping in Furrowe's loft since the barley, and a man in Furrowe's loft is nobody's business. But Furrowe hasn't said anything yet, and Ilo doesn't know if he will, and a man with no paper who's found in the barns at a count is a hand.
So he's in the ditch behind the end barn, in the dark, under the hawthorn, lying flat in a foot of black water with the cold coming up through his shirt. He's been there since he heard the gate.

He gave his bread at supper to Davin, because Davin was coughing and eats when he's coughing. So he's had a cup of the oats at five in the morning and nothing since, and his stomach has gone past growling into a slow ache like a fist pressed in under the ribs, and the cold is getting into the ache and making it worse.
Pruett. Five. Where's the grandmother?
She's in the corner, Dad. She's asleep.
Wake her up. I'm not counting her by the smell.

The water's in his ears. He can hear the count through it, name by name, and Pilot snuffling along the barn wall, and the dog's chain. His feet went numb half an hour ago and he can't feel if they're still in his boots. His jaw keeps going and he holds it shut with his hand so his teeth won't click.
Pilot comes round the end of the barn. Ilo hears him stop.
The dog goes in. He goes into the hawthorn and into the water, and gets Ilo by the forearm, the left, through the shirt, and pulls.

Ilo doesn't shout. He gets his right hand round the dog's muzzle and holds it shut with the dog's teeth still in his arm, and lies there in the water holding it, and the dog shakes its head to get a better grip, and every time it shakes he can feel the teeth go further in, and he holds it.
It's quiet, the whole thing. The water slaps. That's all.
Pilot. What's he got.
Rats, Dad. He's got a rat.
Josh whistles. The dog lets go, the way a trained dog lets go, all at once, and backs out of the hawthorn with its muzzle wet and dark, and goes to his boot.
The lantern comes to the end of the barn, and stops, and swings once over the ditch. Will is holding it. He looks straight at the hawthorn for a long time. Then he turns round with it.
Nothing, Dad. It's a rat hole.

Ilo stays in the water an hour after the gate shuts. When he gets up he can't stand, and he crawls the last of it to Furrowe's yard on his hands and knees, with his left arm held up against his chest because there's a flap of skin on it the size of a penny that opens and shuts when he moves his fingers.

Abel's hayloft, over the horse, after the count, past midnight. One lantern on a nail. Ilo Haldane, who was Ilo then and nothing else, sits on a bale with a horse blanket round him that stinks of horse, and his wet things spread over the bales to steam. He's been sleeping up here since the barley. It's warm from the horse, and he can't get warm.

He shakes. Not shivers, shakes, in long fits that start in his stomach and go out to his hands, and then stop, and then start again. His feet are white and wrinkled like a drowned man's and he's got them pushed down into the hay.
His left forearm is wrapped in a strip torn off a sack, and the sack's gone black through in a patch the size of a hand. He hasn't looked under it.
He has a knife and a piece of pear wood, and he's trying to make a spoon one-handed with the wood held between his knees, because his hands want something to do.

Abel comes up the ladder slowly, because he's sixty-three and the rungs are greasy, and sits down on the top one with his legs still on the ladder, like a boy. He has a heel of bread in his coat pocket and half a cold sausage in a paper, and he puts them on the boards without saying what they are.

Ilo eats the bread first. He eats it too fast and it hurts going down, and he has to stop with his hand flat on his chest and wait, and then he eats the sausage, paper and all nearly, and licks the grease off the paper.
Brack's been round with the dog, then.
He has.
Did it get you.
Something did.
Let's see it.

Ilo unwinds the sacking. The dog's top teeth have gone in in a curve of holes, and the bottom teeth have torn, and there's a flap of skin lifted off the arm like the lid of a tin, and under it it's red and white and wet. Abel looks at it under the lantern for a long time. He has seen a lot of hands' arms.
That wants Lind.
Lind wants a shilling.
Wrap it up, then. Keep it clean. Piss on it if it goes green, my father used to say, and he had both his arms when he died.
That's a good spoon.
It's for the little one. Bet's.
I know whose it's for.
Ilo goes on carving. A curl of pear wood falls off the knife onto his knee.
They passed it today. Seasonal hands aren't resident. First frost, the ones with no roof go back up the hill road. Mott wrote it.
Mott writes everything.
There's the barns at Haldane's. Old Purkiss has gone to his daughter's.
I know whose barns they are.
A tenant's a resident. That's in the rule as well. Mott wrote that too.
And Bet.
Bet wants a husband and the little one wants a name. You want a roof by the frost.
You want it done by Sunday.
I'd like it done by Sunday, yes.
The horse shifts underneath them and the boards creak. Ilo holds the spoon up to the lantern and looks along the handle to see if it's straight. It isn't, quite.
She's a good girl, Bet.
She is.
Your Ned thinks so.
Abel doesn't say anything for a while. He takes his hat off and turns it round in his hands by the brim, looking for something on the band.
Ned's married.
I know. I was at it. I carried the chairs.
So you were.
He'll say yes. He was always going to say yes. You've done him a kindness.
Can I keep the horse company till Sunday, then.
You can keep him company as long as you like.
Abel goes back down the ladder. Ilo finishes the spoon by feel after the lantern's out, and in the morning the bowl of it is crooked and he keeps it anyway.

The Furrowe parlour, the morning after the loft. A good room nobody sits in: a horsehair sofa, a clock under a glass dome, a framed certificate from the exchange with Abel's name in copperplate. The fire's laid and not lit.

Bet Carrow has come in by the back, through the scullery, because that's the way she's always come into this house, since she was fifteen and did the Furrowes' step on a Saturday for sixpence. She has Anni on her hip. She hasn't been asked to sit and she doesn't.
Abel is at the table by the window with an envelope in front of him, square to the edge, and a sheet of paper with figures on it in his own hand.
He's said yes.
I know. He came by ours last night with his arm in a sack and asked my dad for me. My dad laughed at him for a quarter of an hour.
What's wrong with his arm.
You'd have to ask Josh Brack's dog.
Abel looks at the envelope for a while.
The barns at Haldane's, then. The house and the end barn and the paddock. At Purkiss's rent, which was fair, and which I've not put up.
Purkiss paid four and six.
Purkiss paid four and six.
And what else.
There's twelve pound in that for the wedding and the setting up. You'll not need to say where it's from.
Who'd I say it to.
And the little one goes in the book as his. That's a kindness to her, Bet. You know it is. A child wants a name on her paper.

Through the wall, in the back room, Mary Furrowe's baby starts crying, the thin new crying of a baby a week old. Then Mary's voice, low, singing to it. Bet turns her head to the wall and listens to it. Anni turns her head too, because her mother did.
That's Pell.
That's Pell.
He's got a good pair of lungs.
He has.
Bet hitches Anni up her hip. Anni has got hold of Bet's collar and is chewing it.
She'll not come to this house. Not to the front, not to the back. That's what you're paying for. I'm not soft. I did your step for five years.
I'd not put it like that.
You'd not put it any way at all. That's what the twelve pound is.
And Ned's not to come to the barns. Not for the rent. Not for anything. You'll send somebody.
I'll come for the rent myself.
Then you'll come. Not him.
Not him.
She takes the envelope off the table and doesn't open it to count it, which is the thing Abel will remember about her: she didn't count it. She puts it in the front of her dress.
One more thing. The four and six. I want it written that it stays four and six. Whoever has the barns after you. As long as I'm in them.
Four and six for thirty years. The barns'll be worth eight by the time she's forty.
She's a Carrow off the Osby road. She's asking you for a paper.
Say it: The rent's the rent, Bet. It'll be fair. You've my word on it.
Your word. Right.

She goes out by the scullery the way she came. In the passage she stops by the back room door, where the singing is, and stands there with Anni for as long as it takes to say a short prayer, and then goes on.
Abel sits at the table with the sheet of figures, and takes his pencil, and under Purkiss, four and six, writes Haldane, and stops, because it's not a name yet till Friday, and rubs it out.

Edie's room over the draper's, the same afternoon. A dressmaker's dummy with no head, pins in a tin, a long glass with a crack across one corner. Bet is standing on a chair in her good blue, the one Edie let out in the spring of the year before last, being taken back in.
Breathe in.
I am breathing in.
Breathe in like you mean it. You've been eating Furrowe's bread.
I've been eating my dad's bread. It's all chaff.

Edie has pins in her mouth and talks round them. She takes the waist in an inch, and another inch, kneeling on the floor with the hem across her knees. Anni is asleep on Edie's bed on a pile of offcuts.
So it's the hill man.
It's Ilo.
It's Ilo who sings on the rick with his shirt off.
That's him.
Does he know.
Know what.
Edie takes the pins out of her mouth one at a time and puts them in the cushion.
Bet. I let this out in March. I let it out again in May. I know what I let it out for.
Bet looks at herself in the cracked glass for a long time, in the blue dress, standing on a chair, like a statue of somebody.
He knows. He was at the wedding. Ned's. He carried the chairs.
And he's having you anyway.
He's having a roof. Furrowe's giving him the barns and a name in the book, and he'll not go up the hill at the frost. I'm in with the barns. Like the door.
That's a horrible thing to say.
It's what it is, though. He's not daft. He's the least daft man I know. He asked my dad for me with his arm bleeding through a sack, and my dad laughed at him, and he stood there and let him.
Edie gets up off the floor and stands back to look at the waist. It's good. It's the best she's done.
Do you like him.
I like him better than Ned. Ned cried.
When.
When I told him. He sat on my dad's wall and cried, and I had to tell him it'd be all right. Me. Telling him.
She gets down off the chair, careful of the pins.
You'll not say. To anybody. Not your mam, not Will Brack.
Who'd I say it to.
That's what I said to Furrowe.

The harvest supper, in Orme's big barn, the Saturday. One long table down the middle made of trestles and doors, with every family in the Upper Town along it, and lamps on the beams, and a fiddler on a barrel who can only play four tunes and plays them in turn.
New bread, and dripping in a bowl with the brown at the bottom, and a ham that took two men to carry in. Beer in jugs. A pear on every plate, and the children cutting theirs into eight so it lasts.

Edie the seamstress, twenty-two, is across the table from Will Brack. He's trying to tell her something about the post and has got it backwards, and she's laughing at him with her hand over her mouth, and he's gone red to the ears and is laughing as well.
You said the cart was on the pole.
The pole was on the cart. The pole came down on the cart.
Was anyone in it?
A pig.

Further up, Ned Furrowe has his arm along the back of Mary's chair. Mary is feeding the baby under a shawl, Pell, a week old, born at harvest like a good Furrowe. Bet is three places down with Anni on her knee, and Bet doesn't look at Ned once, all night, and that's how you'd know.
Your table. Your town. Look at it.

Out in the yard, through the window, on an upturned crate with a plate on his knees, Ilo. The hands eat in the yard. They always have. There's sheep's-fat bread for the yard and a pot of something, and they've a fire going, and they're singing out there as well, a different song, and the two songs get in each other's way.
George Orme stands up and bangs a spoon on a jug and asks the professor from Arlen to say a few words, as their guest, and the professor stands up with his glass.
I won't keep you. Your registrar's been very kind, and your Mr Orme. And your Mr Furrowe, who weighed me when I came in and found me wanting.
A big laugh. Abel lifts his glass to him, pleased.
To the harvest. To the plain, which I'm told is the best wheat ground between here and the sea.
It is.
And to our friends in the barns. The Hesh temperament. Patient, and cheerful, and never a thought for next year. They'd sing at a funeral.
And the whole barn laughs, warmly, the way you laugh at a dog that's done something clever. Glasses go up along the table like a wave going down a beach.
Listen to the yard.
In the yard the singing has stopped. Ilo has his plate on his knees and a piece of bread halfway to his mouth, and he's looking at the window, and he can see every glass in it.
Leave the glass on the table.

The glass stays on the cloth. Nobody notices. That's the thing. Everyone's drinking, and Calley sits down to a bang of hands on the table, and the fiddler starts up, and not one person in the barn notices a full glass.
Ilo, in the yard, notices. He looks at the glass through the window for a second, and then at whoever it belongs to, and then he eats his bread.
That was all you did. You'll tell yourself about it for years.

Later, when the lamps are low and the children are asleep along the benches like coats, a patch of white in the yard where Ilo was sitting. It's frost, too early. It's gone by the time anyone looks at it again.
Nothing happens that night. Everybody walks home singing. It's a good supper, the best anyone can remember.

The Monday night, the night before the frost, though nobody knows that yet. In the barns at Haldane's. Somebody has got potatoes, a whole sack, off Orme's ground where they were left in the ruts, and they're in the fire in their skins, and the barn smells like nothing else in the world.

Ketti is sitting with Davin's coat across her knees, putting a patch on the elbow from a bit of Arn's old shirt. She bites the thread off. Davin is asleep against her side with his mouth open, and every so often he coughs in his sleep without waking, and she puts her hand on his back till he stops.

Ilo has come over from Furrowe's for the potatoes, with his arm in a strip of sacking. Nobody's asked him about it. He sits by the fire and pokes the potatoes out of the ash with a stick and juggles them from hand to hand, and blows on them, and hands them round.
Ketti. That one's yours. It's the best one.
They're all the same.
That one's the best. I've been watching it.
You've been watching a potato.
Since it went in. Somebody had to.
She splits it with her thumbs and the steam comes up into her face, and she shuts her eyes in it.
My mam used to do them on the hill in the wall. In the hot stones. You'd put them in at dinner and they'd be done by dark and you'd have forgotten them.
Mine as well.
Did yours burn them?
Every time. She'd say it was the stones.
It's never the stones.

Arn says when they go up, at the frost, he'll make her a wall like that at the hut, and she says he said that last year, and he says he'll make it this year, and she says he said that last year as well.

Ketti sings, after. Not loud, not for anybody, a Heshen song about a girl who loses a goat and finds it on the roof, and the barn goes quiet to hear it, and two or three come in on the end where the goat comes down.
There's a white skin on the water bucket by the door when Ilo goes out. He looks at it. He puts his finger through it, and it breaks like paper.

Three days after the supper, an ordinary Tuesday. The first frost. The road post at seven in the morning, white, and the pole furred with it, and the hill behind gone sharp the way it does on a frost, so you can see every wall on it.

The list is pinned to the post board on a nail. Names in Edwin Mott's hand, nice and round. HANDS, SEASONAL, NOT RESIDENT. Twenty-odd names and their households. The hands are in the road below the pole, with their bundles, because they were told to be.
Josh Brack has the list off the nail and is reading it out. He does it the same every year, so it's not like anything. It's like reading the weather.
Pruett. Pruett and four. Up you go, Pruett.
Tesk. The old man's gone up already, has he. Right.
Sallis. Arn. Wife and the lad.
I've work at Orme's till the potatoes are up.
Have you a paper says so?
Mr Orme said.
Mr Orme says a lot of things in August.
The lad's got a cough. Can we not go up Monday?
I don't set the frost, missus.
Davin Sallis, eight, is standing behind his mother's skirt. He coughs into it, a wet cough that goes on too long, and she puts her hand on his head without looking.

Abel Furrowe has come down the road in his trap to see the hands go up, which he does every year, because they are the exchange's hands as much as anybody's. He sits on the box with his hat on and the reins loose.
The loft over the horse takes two at a pinch. One's spoken for.
Sit on the box and watch them go up.

source.words: Sit on the box and watch them go up.

text: Up you go, Sallis.
Arn picks up the big bundle, and Ketti the small one, and Davin a tin kettle on a string. They go through under the pole when Will lifts it, and start up the hill road behind the Pruetts.

From the post, held: the hands going up the hill road in a line, with their bundles on their backs, the way they came down in August, only slower, because it's uphill and it's cold. The frost is going off the road where the sun touches it and staying where it doesn't. Josh stands at the pole with the list.
Halfway up, Ketti Sallis stops to cough, bent over with her hand on her knee, and Arn waits for her with the bundle, and Davin waits with the kettle, and then they go on.
They go over the shoulder of the hill one at a time, and then there's only the road.

The road post, after. The frost is off the road now except in the ruts. The ones who were kept, if there were any, have gone off to wherever they're kept. Josh is pinning Mott's list back on the nail with the crossings-off on it in his pencil.
Will is at the pole. He hasn't let it down. He's looking up the hill road at the shoulder where they went over.
Dad.
Let the pole down.
The Sallis lad was coughing blood. On the frost, by the pole. There's some there. I saw it.
Let the pole down, Will.
I'm only saying we could've had Lind look at him.

Josh turns round from the board with the post book in his hand, a big book bound in board with brass corners, and hits Will across the face with it. Not the flat. The edge, the corner. Will's head goes round and his hat goes in the road again and he takes two steps sideways to keep his feet.

When he straightens up his top lip's split against his teeth and his nose is going, two lines of it down into his mouth and off his chin, onto the front of the coat that was bought big for him. It drips on the frost in the rut, beside the other.
Lind's signed them. Every one. Fit to travel. You want to read his name? It's on the back.
No, Dad.
When I say let the pole down, you let the pole down. When I say go on, they go on. That's the whole of it, Will. That's the whole of the job.

Will lets the pole down. He holds his sleeve under his nose. He doesn't wipe it, he just holds it there, and stands at the pole the way his father stands at it, with his feet apart, looking at the road.

Josh sits down on his bucket and opens the book where he hit him with it, and there's blood on the board of the cover, and he wipes it off with his thumb, and looks at his thumb, and wipes his thumb on his knee.
Abel's trap goes back along the road toward the town. He'd seen it. He touches his hat to Josh going past, and Josh touches his.

The registrar's front counter, the Friday. Census day for the new rule: everybody with a fixed abode comes in and is written down. The queue goes out of the door and along the front of the building and round the corner, and it's raining, and the ones outside hold their coats over their heads.
Edwin Mott at the counter with the big book. Walter beside him with the copy slips, writing his sevens with no bar through them, which his father has told him about twice.
Ilo in the queue with Bet, and Anni asleep on Bet's hip with her thumb in. Ilo has a clean shirt on that he borrowed. He has the crooked spoon in his pocket and keeps touching it.
Stay at home and send Mott a note.
There's a note on the counter by Edwin's elbow, folded, with a good seal on it, and Edwin keeps it under his hand and doesn't open it until it's wanted.
Next. Name.
Ilo.
Surname.
Ilo.
Your other name. Your father's name.
My father was Ilo as well.
Somebody behind them in the queue laughs, and then stops.
I need a surname. The column's for a surname.
We don't have them up there. You're your father's son, that's all. You're Ilo who's Ilo's.
Well, you're down here now. Where are you resident.
The barns at Haldane's. From Sunday.
Edwin takes the note out from under his hand and reads it, and folds it up again.
Edwin dips the pen. His pen is over the column, and Ilo can see it there, waiting, and the queue is waiting, and the rain is coming in round the door.
Put Haldane.
Haldane.
After the farm. Put Haldane.

Edwin writes it. He strikes through ILO in the first column and writes HALDANE, I., and then after it, small, the way he'd note a source: after the farm. Walter copies it onto a slip and blots it and pushes it across the counter.
You saw him decide it. He decided it before the pen came down, so it's his name. That's what you'll say.
Wife.
Bet. Elizabeth. Carrow, it was.
Married when.
Sunday.
The child.
Anni.
Born.
Two years at Lammas.
Father.
Bet doesn't answer. She hitches Anni up her hip. Edwin looks at the note again.

Edwin rules a line through the father column with his ruler, neat, all the way across. Then he takes a pencil out from behind his ear, not the pen, and writes in the margin beside it: per letter, A.F.
Next.

Outside, Ilo unfolds the slip and holds it so the rain won't get it and looks at it a long time, though he can't read it. Bet reads it to him. Then he folds it small and puts it in the inside pocket of the borrowed shirt.
Haldane. Haldane. Haldane.
You'll get used to it.
I'll have to, won't I. It's on a paper.

The Sunday. The wedding is at nine at the Furrow Church, before the service, so the vicar can do it and then do the service, and there are six people at it, and one of them is asleep, and that's Anni.

After, in the barns at Haldane's, the hands who are left have made a table out of planks on two barrels, and there's a ham end from Orme's supper that Edie got from the barn the morning after, and bread, and a cake Bet's mother made with no eggs in it that sinks in the middle like a saddle.

Old Carrow has his fiddle, which is worse than Orme's fiddler's but knows more than four tunes. He plays sitting on a cask with his eyes shut. Ilo dances with Bet in the straw, badly, with his bad arm held up out of the way like a man carrying a tray.
You dance like a hen in a wind.
I dance like a hill man.
That's what I said.

Then Ilo dances with Anni, holding her up, swinging her round till she screams, and puts her down dizzy, and she falls on her bottom in the straw and looks surprised, and gets up and holds her arms up for more.
Bet's mother takes Ilo by the face with both hands in the yard and looks at him a long time, the way you'd look at a horse you'd been sold, and then kisses him on the forehead, hard, and lets go.
Osby fair, the Sunday after the wedding, which was quick and had six people at it. The crockery stall at the end of the row under a striped awning, with bowls stacked up in towers.

Bet has the wedding money in a handkerchief, from Abel, in an envelope with nothing written on it. She picks up the bowls one at a time and taps each one with her nail and listens. She buys five, matched, the blue rim.
Five. There's three of us.
My mam said buy five.
Your mam's not paying for them.
My mam said buy five, Ilo.
He carries them home in the basket on his arm, all the way, with Anni on his shoulders holding his ears.

The barns at Haldane's, the Monday. Old Carrow comes over from the Osby road with a crowbar, and he and Ilo take the big door off the end barn. It comes off the pins with a shriek. It's heavier than either of them thought, and they have to put it down twice crossing the yard, and the second time Carrow sits down on it and laughs till he coughs.
You're marrying my girl and you're stealing a door off Furrowe.
It's my door. I rent it.
Since Sunday.
Since Sunday.
Bet stands in the kitchen doorway with Anni and the basket of bowls and doesn't help, and tells them they're doing it wrong. The hinge pins stay in the barn wall, with nothing on them.

The Haldane kitchen. The table, new, made of a barn door on four legs, with the hinge marks still in it where Ilo couldn't plane them out. On one of the legs, low down, where you'd only see it if you were a child, Ilo has carved a goat with its head turned back over its shoulder, the way they carve them on the hill.
Three bowls on the table. Three places. Bread, and a little dripping, and an apple for Anni cut small.
Two bowls on the shelf over the stove, turned over, so the dust won't get in them. For whoever comes.
Ilo puts the crooked spoon by Anni's bowl. She picks it up and bangs the table with it. She does it again, and he laughs.
You know this table.

That winter. The hut at the top of the hill road, in the lee of the long wall, December. One room of stone with a turf roof and a door made of three planks and a sack, and snow on the turf, and snow on the wall, and snow on the door where it blows in under the sack.
Davin's snare has a hare in it. He brings it in by the back legs, stiff, frozen, with snow in its fur, and holds it up with both arms like a thing he made himself.
Mam. Mam. Look.
Oh, look at that. Look at him. Arn, look what he's got.
He never.
I did. In the gap by the thorn. Where you said.
Where your dad said and you said it was daft.

Ketti skins it on the doorstep with Arn's knife, quick, the way you'd take off a glove, and the steam comes off the meat in the cold. Her fingers are raw and split at every knuckle and the cracks open when she bends them and she doesn't notice.

They stew it with the last of the oats and a bit of the dripping, and it takes all afternoon because the fire's peat and wet, and they sit round it in their coats and blankets watching the pot. When it's done they eat it with their fingers out of the one tin, the three of them, burning their mouths.
That's the best thing I've ever had. That is. I'm not having it said it isn't.
You said that about Ilo's potato.
That was the best potato. This is the best thing.
Davin falls asleep with a bone in his hand. Ketti takes it out of his fingers and sucks it, and puts it on the fire.
She coughs in the night, the first time. Arn hears it and lies still and counts it.

January. The snow is up to the eaves on the wall side and the door won't shut on it any more. They burn the stool. They burn the snare pegs. Arn goes down the hill road as far as the shoulder every morning to look at the plain and comes back.

Ketti has had Davin's cough for three weeks and it's gone down into her. She lies on the bed of bracken by the fire under every coat they have, and she's hot, though there's ice on the inside of the walls, so hot that the snow melts where her hand hangs down onto it.

When she coughs it comes up red. Not a speck. A mouthful, dark and frothy, and she turns her head to the wall to do it so the boy won't see, and Arn wipes the wall with snow after, and the snow goes pink and he throws it out of the door.

Her lips are split in three places and gone a grey colour at the edges. Her feet are the worst. The toes on the left have gone black at the ends, hard and black like burnt wood, and they smell, and she can't feel them. Arn has her feet inside his shirt, against his belly, both of them, and he sits like that all day with his back against the wall.
Arn.
I'm here.
Is it the sun.
It's the middle of the night, love.
You owe me a penny.
I owe you a penny.

Davin is asleep against her side, under the coats, the way she used to sleep against her mother. Every time she coughs he wakes and puts his hand on her the way she used to put hers on him, and goes back to sleep.
Did you make the wall.
I'll make it in the spring.
For the potatoes.
For the potatoes. In the hot stones.
You'll burn them.
I'll burn them.
It's never the stones.
She goes quiet after that. Her breathing goes on a long time, a wet rattle like stirring gravel, slower, and then there's a gap in it that goes on, and then one more breath, and then there isn't one.

Arn sits with her feet in his shirt till the fire goes down. He knows. He doesn't move. When the fire goes down to red he can see her face, and her mouth's open a bit, and there's frost coming on her eyelashes already because she's not warm any more to stop it.
He said he didn't set the frost. Brack. He said that.
In the morning Davin wakes up because his mother is cold. He lies there a while with his hand on her before he says anything.
Dad. Mam's gone cold.
I know, son. Come here. Come here to me.

The ground is iron. Arn can't dig it. He carries her out in the blanket and lays her in the lee of the long wall, and he takes the stones off the top of the wall, one at a time, and lays them over her, all day, till you can't see the blanket. He doesn't stop to eat. Davin carries the small ones.
It's a wall, when it's done. A short wall, against the long wall, the length of a woman.
Josh Brack read the name off a list on a Tuesday, and went home for his tea.
Years on. The Sheaf, Mill Street, on a winter evening, the back room. It's rent night, and the window behind Ilo is black with the cold.

Ilo Haldane is at the back table with a half he's made last since six. Tomas has been sent to fetch him home and has sat down on the bench instead, in a brown coat too big for him with the cuffs turned back twice.
Mr Furrowe is at the end of the back table, old now, with the rent book open and the coins in stacks. A Hesh tenant doesn't knock at the Furrowe front door. The rent comes to the Sheaf.
Why's it Haldane, though. Why's it not something proper.
What's proper.
Something that's a name. Pruett. Sallis.
Ilo goes in his coat and gets out a bit of paper folded so small and so often it's gone soft, like cloth, and puts it on the table, and opens it out flat with the side of his hand.
That's your name. That's where it come from. Read it me.
Haldane, I. After the farm.
After the farm.
I know it's because of the farm. Why'd you let him?
There was a queue right out the door, and it was raining.
That's not why.
Mr Furrowe sent a letter. He didn't come. Mott had it under his hand the whole time like a card he was keeping.
I had the horse to see to.
Ilo looks at the old man for a second, and doesn't say anything to that.
I said put Haldane. I said it. He had the pen over the paper. I thought, if it's going on there anyway, I'll be the one that said it.
They'd a meeting up at the registrar's. Mr Furrowe told me after, in the loft. Hands aren't resident. First frost, if you've no roof, you go back up.
Up the hill?
Up the hill. In October.
And a tenant's resident. That was in it as well. So I was a tenant by the Sunday.
There was a supper. Orme's big barn. We ate in the yard, we always ate in the yard. You could see in through the window. A ham the size of you.
Did you get any?
I got the fat off it. There was a man from Arlen made a speech, and they all laughed.
What did he say?
He said we'd sing at a funeral.
The men at the next table have heard it. One of them laughs, and stops.
We would, though.
We would. That's why it was funny.
Every glass in that barn went up but one. I don't know why I remember that. Nobody else noticed.
Old Tesk told me this one. His Kel swept the mill. Took a bit of barley off the floor in his boots for his dad's chest.
Orme had him walked to the post in his bare feet with his boots in his hands. They put the barley in a bag and wrote on it. Barred off the plain. He's never been down since.
For sweepings.
That's what Tesk said. For sweepings.
The first frost, they read the list at the post. Every name. I went down to see them off, the Sallises and the Pruetts.
Mr Brack read it. He read it like he was reading the price of oats.
Arn and Ketti went up with the rest. And the lad, Davin. Ketti stopped halfway up to cough and Arn waited for her.
Ilo turns his glass round on the table, a quarter turn at a time.
Dorrah told me at the cup, in the spring. Ketti died up there in the winter. In January. In the hut at the top, with the snow on the door.
Of the cough?
Of the cold. Of the cough. Of up there. Arn came down the next harvest with just the lad.
At the end of the table, Mr Furrowe goes on counting the coins into stacks. He loses his count and starts the stack again.
And then I married your mum. And we went to Osby fair with the money and she bought the bowls. And me and your grandad Carrow took the door off the end barn for the table, and we dropped it twice.
Why five bowls, when there was only three of you?
Your gran said buy five.
Why?
Because then there was you, and then there was Aaron. Two on the shelf, turned over, waiting. And then you came, and then he came, and that was all of them.
Mum says come now. You're to mind the yard.
I'm to mind the yard.

Mr Furrowe finishes the count and writes it in the book. Then he takes one coin off the last stack and pushes it back across the table toward Ilo with one finger, without a word. Ilo leaves it where it is. Tomas looks at the coin, and then at his dad, and then at the coin.
A kitchen, a long time after. A tin on the oilcloth with the lid off, and a girl of about twelve taking the papers out of it one at a time and laying them in a row.
What's all these?
Put them back the way they were. They go in order.
The woman at the stove has a long careful face, and a blue thread round her wrist so old it has gone the colour of string.
Of what, though?
Anni comes over and puts the lid on the tin, and keeps her hand flat on it.
Ask me when you're older.
Winter. Edrin, the Upper Town.
Ned Furrowe's day. Abel's son. District inspector now. He signs the returns.

source.words: Stay at home and send Mott a note.

text: From the bell tower, before it is light. Frost on the slates of Exchange Street, and smoke from about one chimney in four.

The relief queue starts at the office door and goes round three sides of the square. People stand close for the warmth. Nobody talks. A woman near the back is holding a child who is too big to be held, and every so often she shifts him to the other hip.

On the fourth side, under the lamps of the goods yard, the export train. Soldiers stand along it with their rifles slung while men load sacks stencilled HALVARD GRAIN CO. In the queue, heads turn to watch every sack go up, and turn back.

Past the church, on the hill's shoulder, the burial ground. The new rows are on the left, where the ground was soft enough to dig in October. Since the frost they have been leaving the coffins in the church porch.

On the far side of the square, on the first floor over the relief office, the returns-room window, dark. The queue starts directly under it. Ned Furrowe has stood at that window most mornings this winter with his coffee and has never once looked straight down.
You could count them from here, if you wanted the figure. You go down the back stairs.
Go down to the returns room.

The returns room. On the wall, the district map, the eleven villages in Ned Furrowe's own hand and an ink figure beside each. Under some of the ink, if you stand close, there is a smaller figure in pencil.

The stove went out in the night. He has his coat on and his gloves off, because you can't hold a pen in gloves. The good hat is on the hook by the door, and under it his father's blackthorn stick, which Ned has carried on the hill roads since Abel's knees went.
Morning, Mr Furrowe. Krall's End and the barns. Sorry they're late. My lad's got the cough. I was up with him.
Walter Mott puts two return sheets on the desk and stands back from them.
KRALL'S END. YIELD 340. W. MOTT, BRIGADE CLERK.
HALDANE BARNS. YIELD 310. W. MOTT, BRIGADE CLERK.
The three on the barns sheet is darker than the one and the nought.
It's the dry cough, is it, or the wet?
Coughing. They're all coughing. He'll be all right. They've chalked the Pruetts' door, next but one. That's the fever, that is. That's not a cough.
Mott scratches at his wrist under the cuff, and catches himself doing it, and puts the hand in his pocket.
Ask him what the barns brought in.
What it says, Mr Furrowe.
Three-ten. That's what it says.
He is looking at the map, at the barns, at the pencil under the ink.
Against the window the sheet goes thin. Under the three there is a one. Under the one there is a nine. The nought is a nought.
That's a blot. The nib went. I went over it.
You went over a hundred and ninety with three hundred and ten.
Mott takes his hat off and holds it in both hands. It's an old hat, and the brim is coming away at the back.

Everyone's writing three hundred. Moor Holt wrote three-twenty. If I send in a hundred and ninety, they'll have me in that office in front of the Commissioner, and they'll ask me where the rest went, and what do I say? Jonah Krall's had his photograph in the paper.
I've three at home. Mrs Mott's been giving hers to the little one since November. I can see her collarbones through her dress.
Sorry. That's not your business. Sorry.
A hundred and ninety. It's on your own map in pencil from September. You counted that barn yourself, with the girl reading the tally off the cart.
Pencil a hundred and ninety beside his three-ten, the way you always do.
Small, under the ink, the way he does it every time:
Nobody reads the pencil. Nobody has ever asked him about the pencil.
Will that go anywhere?
It's pencil, Walter.
Mott nods a long time, as if that were an answer.
He signs the bottom of both sheets.
Received and found correct. N. Furrowe, District Inspector.
The sheet says three-ten. You've signed that the sheet says three-ten. Nobody can say you didn't.
Mott puts his hat back on and goes. On the stairs he coughs, and it isn't the cold.
A knock, a quiet one, the kind you make when you don't want to be heard knocking.

A boy in the corridor with his cap in both hands, in a brown coat with a patch on the front, made for somebody bigger. The cuffs are turned back twice. His hair is braided and tucked into the back of his collar. There's a blue thread round his left wrist, and he keeps his right hand over it.
Mr Furrowe? Sorry. They said downstairs you'd be in. Tomas Haldane. From the barns. Mum doesn't know I've come.
You knew my dad. Ilo. He did two summers for your father when he first came down, before I was born. He still talks about your father's hat.
He laughs, a short one, and stops it.
Tomas. What is it?
They came Monday with a paper. Anni read it out. It says we owe them sacks. We haven't got any sacks. They took all ours in October.
He takes a folded sheet out of his coat. Columns of fives, ticked through, in a girl's careful hand.
Sacks to the cart, October. [tally:190] 190. Anni H.
My sister counted them onto the cart. Every one. She counts everything, she drives Mum mad.
And the Gazette's saying it's under the goats. The Hesh have got it in holes up on Tesk's hill. That's Mrs Tesk's place. My mum's friend. They're sending the squad up there next, everybody says.
If you came up and looked. If you wrote it down that there's no hole. They'd believe you. You've got the paper with your name on.
Leave the tally with me.
You'll want it back to her, though. She'll want it back. She keeps them all in a tin.
It'll be in my inside pocket. With the pen.
The sheet goes into the inside pocket of his coat, with the pen.
The district meeting room. A long table with a green cloth on it, and the eleven chairmen down both sides with their coats on, because the stove is lit but there isn't enough coal in it to matter.
At the head, Commissioner Pask, from Arlen, with a cold. He has a plate of biscuits in front of him and doesn't offer them. Nobody looks at the biscuits.
Sorry. This chest. Right. Krall's End.
Three hundred and forty, Commissioner.
Jonah Krall says it standing up, the way you'd say it in church. Somebody starts to clap and two others join in because the first one did.
Three-forty. On that ground. That's what I want the capital to see, that. That's a man who's been listening.

Now. I'll be plain, because I'm tired. Every sack this plain sends up keeps a factory in Arlen open, and every factory buys a tractor from Halvard in the spring, and the tractors are what stop this happening next winter. That's the deal. I didn't make it and I'm not going to apologise for it to men in coats.
So when I hear a low figure, I don't hear weather. I hear somebody's got grain somewhere they're not telling me about.
Inspector. The district.

The district sheet in front of him, in his own hand. At the bottom, the total of what the villages sent: two hundred and ninety. On the map in the returns room, in pencil, under every ink figure, there is the other one. Added up in his head on the stairs this morning, it comes to two hundred and five.
Two-ninety is what they sent. You only add up what they send. That's the whole of the job, and you've done it right for eleven years.
Mott's three is under the two-ninety. So is Krall's whole sheet.
Two hundred and ninety, as the villages reported.

source.words: Two hundred and ninety, as the villages reported.

text: Two-ninety. Fine. Low, but fine. Sign there.
The pen they give you for the district sheet is the good one, black, with a gold band. He signs with it. Somebody pats his shoulder on the way out.
You reported as found.
The meeting breaks up into coats and coughing. Out on the square the relief queue has hardly moved since the morning.
The Sheaf on Mill Street, at dinner time. Ned goes in for a brandy, which he never does in the day, and stands at the end of the bar with his hat on so as not to stop.

There's no beer worth the name. There's a jug of something brown and thin on the back table, and six men round it who have had no work since the mill shut, making one half-pint last an hour. A pickled egg on a saucer, cut in four, and nobody has had their quarter yet.
Ilo Haldane is at the back table with his cap pushed up. He's telling it again, the one they all know, and they let him, because he tells it well.
So he says, name. I say, Ilo. He says no, your name. I say, that is my name. He writes Haldane.

The door goes, and the cold comes in with a boy in a brown coat too big for him. Tomas, sent to fetch his dad, with the cuffs turned back twice. He sits down on the bench by the door like he always does and waits to be noticed.
Because of the farm.
Because of the farm. I was named after a barn, lads.
You were named after a barn and you've been trying to live up to it ever since.

It goes round the table. A man called Sallis laughs so hard he has to put his head down on his arms, and then the whole table's gone, and the landlord's laughing behind the bar without knowing why. Tomas sits there looking pleased with himself, and then he laughs as well, and his laugh sets them off again.
Come here. Come here, you.
Ilo gets him by the back of the neck and pulls him in and gives him the quarter of egg, his own quarter, and Tomas eats it in one go and makes a face, because it's mostly vinegar.
That's horrible.
That's an egg. Your grandmother would have walked to Osby for that.
Mum says come now. The cart's going at one. You're to mind the yard.
I'm to mind the yard.
She says a Hesh man on a cart at the post is a reason.
The table goes quiet, not unkindly. It's what they all know too. Ilo finishes the thin brown stuff in the jug and puts his cap straight.
Sul ve ama. Off we go.

Outside, the pump at the end of Mill Street, with women in a line for it holding buckets. There's chalk on the pump's iron, in a council hand: BOIL ALL WATER. BY ORDER. Under it, in a different hand, bigger: ASK THE WELL WHY.
Two doors down, a white cross chalked on a door, and a ribbon tied to the knocker. The fever. Somebody has left a loaf on the step for them, and nobody will go near enough to knock.
They wash their dead in it up there. In the Well. Everybody knows. And where do you think it comes down to.
Iris Krall, in good gloves, in the line for water she doesn't need, because the pump is where you hear things.
The Commissioner sends him out to the post to countersign the day's requisition tally. A mile of frozen road. He walks it with his collar up.
At the barrier there's a cart, and he knows it before he can see the faces, because of the girl standing up in the back.
A barrier pole across the road, a brazier, a hut. Sergeant Brack with his hands in his armpits, and a constable going through the Haldanes' cart with a bayonet, pushing it into the sacks.
Aaron at the horse's head, looking at nothing. The mother, Bet, on the bench. The girl stands in the back between the sacks, counting them out loud as the constable lifts each one down.
Four. That's four. You've had four.
Anni. Sit down.
He's had four, Mum. I'm only saying it so somebody's said it.

Two sacks are left on the cart. Seed, Bet says, to the sergeant, to nobody. The barley for the spring. Brack doesn't look at her. He looks at his boots, then at Ned, and something in his face goes careful.
Inspector.
No pass for the line. Moving grain out of the district. That's hoarding, by the order. You'll want to sign for it.
We were taking it to my sister's at Osby. For the mill there. Ours is shut.
Then she can come and get it with a pass, missus.

It's only for the board, Mrs Haldane. It's only so it's written down somewhere. It's only four, and it's only till the review, and the review's only, it's only, Aaron, hold the horse, will you, he's going to go.
A trap comes up the road behind them from the town, a good pony and a rug over the knees. Mary Furrowe, on her way to her sister's at Tarn Hollow, with a basket and a pass.
Is that Bet's girl?
Go on to Lil's. You'll lose the light.
She'll be fourteen.
I wouldn't know.
March. She was fourteen in March.

Brack lifts the pole for the trap without asking to see the pass. He knows the hat on her husband. The Haldanes wait in the road while she goes through, and Mary doesn't look back at them, and the girl doesn't stop counting.
Look at the girl.
She's standing in the back of the cart between the sacks with her lips moving. A long face, careful, too old for it. The thread at her wrist has gone grey with handling.
Fourteen in March.
The girl isn't counting for the sergeant. She's counting for you, because you're the one with the pen.
Write down the girl's count in your book before you sign.
In the back of his notebook, where he keeps the pencil figures:
Haldane cart, at the post. Six sacks, four taken.
The girl watches him write it.
Six. Not five. There were six.
Six.
Then he signs the board.

The post road, walking back. Two sacks on the cart, the seed, and the horse pulling like it's six. Aaron at its head. Bet on the bench. Anni in the back, sitting now. Tomas walking alongside with his hand on the tailboard.
He had a bayonet and he was scared of Anni. Did you see him? He was scared of a girl with a sum.
He went red.
He went red as a brick. Don't you get clever, he says. I'll get clever if I want.
Four. They had four. I'm telling Dad four.
You'll tell your dad nothing till he's had his tea.
Kesh, ahna. Look at the horse. He knows he's going home.
Tarnish on the road.
There's nobody on the road.
There's always somebody on the road.

There isn't. There's the plain, white both ways, and the hut behind them getting smaller. Aaron stops to fix his boot. His ankles have come up over the tops of them again, and when Bet gets down and presses her thumb into his shin the dent stays there after she takes it away.
It doesn't hurt.
I know it doesn't.
Nine words for rain, and the Tarn have got one, and it's wet.
That's Dad's.
It's mine now. He's had it long enough.
Aaron laughs, and then Anni does, and Bet says Kesh, the both of you, and she's laughing too, under it, with her hand still round Aaron's ankle.

The Furrowes' kitchen. Four at the table and one plate more than there is food for: a stew that is mostly turnip, and half a loaf from the relief office that Mary queued four hours for. She has put the heel on Abel's plate because it's the softest.
Elbows. Pell, elbows. Your father didn't sit at his own table forty years to watch you eat like a Hesh.
I'm eating.
You're shovelling. Pass your grandad the salt, he can't reach.
I can reach.
He can't reach. There.
Ned, tell them about the inspector.
It's only the returns, Mary. There's nothing to tell.
He signed the district today. The whole district. They gave him the good pen.
It's a pen.
Your figure was low, I heard.
It's what the villages sent in, Dad. That's my figure.
Krall's district sent in three hundred and forty. You sent in two-ninety. That's a man standing in the office with his hat in his hands next spring.
Two-ninety is what they sent in. I add up what they send in.

You know where the rest is. Up the hill in a hole under some old woman's goats. They've done it since my father's time. They don't think of it as stealing. That's the thing you have to understand about them, it isn't wickedness, they've just got no word for it.
Mr Tamm says they've got a word for everything. He says their language has nine words for rain.
Has it. Nine words for rain and none for thank you.
Dad.
I'm only saying. I'm fond of them. I had a Hesh lad worked for me two summers, Ilo, lovely lad, sang all day. I'd have trusted him with my life. Not with my grain.
Ned has the girl's tally in his inside pocket. He can feel the fold of it against his chest when he breathes.
Ned, eat something. You've not touched it.
Tell them about the Haldanes' cart.
There was a cart at the post. The Haldanes. Ilo's.
Ilo.
I counted that barn myself in September. There was nothing in it.
That's a good barn, that. I put him in that barn.
I know you did, Dad.
The girl was stood in the back counting the sacks off. Out loud. Four, she said. You've had four. Like she was keeping score for somebody.
He laughs, and it comes out wrong, and he picks his spoon up and puts it down again.

And I'm stood there in my coat with the good pen. Received and found correct. I signed for it, Dad. I sign everything. I'm very good at it. Ask anyone in the building, they'll tell you, Ned Furrowe, lovely clear signature.
Ned.
She's fourteen. Pell's age, near enough.
I'm twelve.
I know you're twelve.
Nobody says anything. Abel cuts the heel of the bread in half and puts half on Ned's plate, and Ned looks at it.
Eat that.
The district granary on Exchange Square, the one the paper photographs. Inside, by one lantern, sacks to the rafters in rows, each one stencilled for the morning train: HALVARD GRAIN CO., VIA ARLEN.
Captain Holt, two guards with rifles, and the bar across the big double door, which is a beam of oak as thick as a man.
Ned is here to count the stock for the train, with his book.
Outside, the sound starts as feet on the frozen square and turns into voices. Then a fist on the door. Then a lot of fists.
Krall's End. They've walked it. Eleven mile in that.
He sounds almost impressed.
Mud-hands. My mother was one. I know exactly what they've got, which is nothing, and what they'll do with it, which is that door.
Through the gap where the doors meet, lanterns, and faces, and breath going up. A woman holding up a child so the guards can see it.
Bet Haldane, near the front. Tomas has got in ahead of her, right up at the door, with his cap off and his braid out, for once, down his back.
We're not here to steal! We want what's ours! You had every sack we grew!
Bar, Sergeant. Get your backs on it.
Read the true figure through the gap in the door. Out loud, so they can all hear it.
He gets the book out. His hands are cold and the pages stick. He has to put his mouth right to the gap, and the wood's frozen and takes skin off his lip.
District inspector. Furrowe. Listen. Krall's End. Krall's End grew a hundred and ninety. Not three-forty. A hundred and ninety.
The Haldane barns. A hundred and ninety. Tesk's fold on the hill. No store. I went up. There's nothing up there but rock and goats.
That's not what you said to the Commissioner.
No. I gave him two-ninety.
Outside it goes quieter, not quiet. Somebody says, what did he say? and somebody else says it back to them, louder.

source.words: Read the true figure through the gap in the door. Out loud, so they can all hear it.

text: Holt looks at the gap, and at the sacks, and at the stencils on the sacks. You can see him doing a sum, and it's not about grain. It's about who was out there to hear that, and whether the Gazette's woman with the camera is one of them.
One sack a family. Krall's End only. Against the review. Your names on it, not mine.
And they go home tonight. All of them.

The bar comes off. The guards hand sacks out through the gap one at a time and people take them without saying anything and go. Bet Haldane takes one and holds it against her like a child. Nobody thanks anybody.
The same hour, the other side of the door. Bet Haldane, with Anni's wrist in her hand so the girl can't get to the front.

Tomas let go of her coat in the crush by the pump, and now he's up at the front somewhere with his braid out down his back. She told him to keep it in his collar. He has the Orme lad's coat on, the brown one with the patch, the cuffs turned back twice, because his own went on the cart in October.
There's sixty-three of us. I've done it twice, Mum.
Hush.
I'm only saying it so somebody's said it.
Count yours. Anni. Aaron by the lamp post.
Somebody inside starts saying numbers through the gap, too fast, a man's voice with a cold in it. The ones at the front go quiet to hear. The ones at the back push.
One of the numbers is a hundred and ninety. She has never heard it said out loud by anybody but Anni.

Then the bar comes off and they hand sacks out through the gap like it was their idea all along. She gets one. It is heavier than she thought, and she nearly drops it, and a soldier holds the other end for a second until she's got it.
He'll want thanking. They always want thanking.
She doesn't say it. She'll not say it.
Stay, and see who it was.

She sends Anni home with Aaron and stays until the square is empty and the frost has come back on the cobbles. Somebody's shawl is frozen to them by the door. It isn't hers. She knows whose it is, and doesn't pick it up.
Nobody comes out of the granary. Nobody says a name to her. A corporal asks her what she wants and she says nothing, nothing, she's going.
At home she takes the bowls off the shelf for the morning, and lays them out, and she doesn't count them, because Anni will.
That night, in the chair by the stove with his boots still on, because the bed is too cold to get into and there's no coal to spare for the bedroom.

r: The Haldanes' table, the barn door with its hinge marks. Bet laying out bowls for the morning. She lays them all but one. She keeps hold of that one and says it's only till the lambing, and goes on holding it.

text: The Haldanes' table, the barn door with its hinge marks. Bet laying out bowls for the morning. She lays them all but one. She keeps hold of that one and says it's only till the lambing, and goes on holding it.
You've seen that table. That's where this is going, and you knew it before you sat down.
You've been up since before five, and you fell asleep in your boots. That's all that was.
Thursday. The returns room. The stove's lit for once, because the Commissioner is coming up later.
Walter Mott isn't at his desk. A boy from the brigade office brings the sheets up instead, and says Mr Mott's got the fever in the house, and they've chalked the door.
A week later. Haldane Yard.
The kitchen in the old hands' barn: a table Ilo made out of a door, a stove, and the shelf over it, bare.
In each bowl a heel of the bread from the granary sack, and hot water with salt in it, which Bet calls soup.
Ilo, Bet, Tomas, Aaron, Anni. Everybody's bowl is on the table.
That's everybody.
It is. Eat.
Nobody says anything else. They eat slowly, to make it last, and Anni counts the turnip in her bowl, under her breath, and doesn't say the number.
The Furrowe table. The bowls full, or full enough. The good pen on the dresser where Mary can see it from the stove.
Iris Krall says Jonah's to be district chairman. She says they'll want a new inspector for the whole plain by the summer, and who else would they ask.
That's the hat, that is. That's my hat on your head.
Ned eats. He eats all of it.

Anni's kitchen, years later. The same oilcloth. The tin on the table with the lid off and the papers out in a row. Anni is forty, and her daughter is twelve, and it's raining, the fine kind that soaks you.
What's all these?
Tallies. Put them back the way they were, they go in order.
Of what, though?
That one's sacks. That's lamps, Exchange Street, all the way down.
Why?
So somebody had.

A knock at the door. An old man with a housing form from the allocation office in a brown envelope, come about the back room, because somebody has to come about the back room. He has his hat in his hand.
Anni lets him in out of the rain and gives him tea in the good cup, and he sits at the end of the table, and she goes on with her daughter as if he were the coal man.
You know this table. You know the hinge marks.
They came on the Monday with a paper. I read it out, because Mum couldn't and Dad couldn't. It said we owed them sacks. There was a name signed at the bottom with a good pen.
The sheet says three-ten. You've signed that the sheet says three-ten. Nobody can say you didn't.
Your uncle Tomas took it into town. He didn't tell Mum. He thought if somebody looked, they'd see.
We took the cart to the post with what was left. Six sacks. I counted them off out loud while the constable put his bayonet in them.
He wrote my number down in his book. I watched him write it. Then he signed the board anyway.
A lady came through in a trap with a rug on her knees. She had a pass. She looked at me and told him I'd be fourteen. Like she was telling him something.
The old man at the end of the table puts his cup down.
The men at the store said everybody's figure went to Arlen high that winter, and the requisition came for it. Nobody said whose.
Who was it?
A man in a coat.
That night the whole of Krall's End walked in to the granary. Mum had my wrist so I couldn't get to the front.
Somebody inside started saying numbers through the gap in the door. Mum said she'd only ever heard me say a hundred and ninety before that night.
They gave out a sack a family through the gap, and nobody said thank you.
Two-ninety is what they sent. You only add up what they send. That's the whole of the job, and you've done it right for eleven years.
That week we were all at the table. All of us. I remember thinking that was a thing that could stop.
The girl has the last paper out of the tin, a copy from the register gone soft at the folds, with a line ruled through one of the columns and something in pencil in the margin.
Who's this, where it's crossed out?
That's where my father goes.
So who was he?
Ilo carried me on his shoulders to Osby fair, the year they bought the bowls.
That's not what I asked.
No.
Say your name.
Furrowe. With an e.
I know how it's spelt.
She pours him more tea. He hadn't finished the first.
Can I take the tin to school? Miss is doing the hard winter this term. She wants things from home.
I'll think about it.
The old man is still at the end of the table, with the cup in both hands, and it's gone cold.
